title: India's New Zealand Tour Sells 50,000 Tickets in Two Weeks
excerpt: NZ Cricket sold more than 50,000 tickets in just over two weeks for India's first tour in six years, reopening Eden Park's sixth tier for the first time since 2019.
body:
• New Zealand Cricket has sold more than 50,000 tickets for the home summer in just over two weeks, driven by India's first tour in six years.
  • The 12-match all-format tour — 5 T20Is, 5 ODIs and 2 Tests — runs from October 22 to December 1, the longest inbound tour in New Zealand Cricket history.
  • Demand has forced NZC to open Eden Park's sixth tier of seating for the first time since India's 2019 tour, while the second T20I at Hagley Oval is already 75% sold.
  • The tour carries added heat from the March T20 World Cup final in Ahmedabad, where India beat New Zealand by 96 runs for a record third title.

New Zealand Cricket has sold more than 50,000 tickets for the home summer in just over two weeks of sales, with officials saying the rush is being driven overwhelmingly by India's first tour of the country in six years.

The figures, confirmed by NZC on September 9, came after a record-breaking two-week pre-sale for Cricket Nation members, Sky and ANZ customers, followed by the first days of general public sale on September 7. Tim Ellis, NZC's head of marketing, said demand had been so strong that the board had been forced to open the sixth tier of seating at Eden Park in Auckland for the fourth T20I on October 30 — the first time that tier has been used since India last toured in 2019, and only a handful of times in recent years, including the 2015 World Cup.

The tour: 12 matches, seven weeks

India's tour, announced in June, is the most international matches ever scheduled for an inbound New Zealand tour: five T20Is from October 22 to November 1, five ODIs from November 4 to 15, and two Tests from November 19 to December 1. The series is backed by the New Zealand government, which is marking it alongside other India sporting tours as part of 100 years of New Zealand–India sporting ties.

The T20Is open with a double-header at Hagley Oval in Christchurch on October 22 and 24 before moving to Wellington's HNRY Stadium, Eden Park in Auckland, and Seddon Park in Hamilton. The ODIs visit Auckland, Wellington, Hamilton and Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui. The two Tests — at Wellington's Basin Reserve and Christchurch's Hagley Oval — form part of the 2025–27 World Test Championship cycle, and matter for India, who sit sixth in the standings and need results to stay in contention for the final.

Sales records fall

The early numbers were historic even before public sale began. NZC reported 26,000 tickets sold in the first 48 hours of the members' pre-sale — a record-breaking start for an international summer. By early September the tally had crossed 50,000, with the October 22 opener still 43 days away.

Some matches are approaching sell-out. The second T20I at Hagley Oval, a ground with a capacity of just 9,000, is more than three-quarters sold — "quite remarkable," in Ellis's words. Wellington's fixtures at HNRY Stadium and the Basin Reserve have also shown strong early sales, and NZC deliberately held prices flat with last season: under NZ$30 a ticket with the Cricket Nation access code, plus pre-sale discounts and group packages.

Why the frenzy

Part of the demand is simple scarcity — six years since India last toured, and a squad expected to include Virat Kohli and Jasprit Bumrah. "This is a rare chance for Kiwis to experience the incredible buzz of a game of cricket involving India and watch some of the biggest sport stars on the planet compete," NZC chief marketing and commercial officer Glenn Critchley said when the schedule was announced.

The other part is narrative. India and New Zealand met in the 2026 ICC Men's T20 World Cup final in Ahmedabad on March 8, when India won by 96 runs — 255 for 5 against New Zealand's 159 all out — in front of 86,824 spectators, for a record third T20 world title. This tour is the first bilateral meeting since that night, and NZC is leaning into the rematch.

A rivalry with recent history

India's recent tours of New Zealand have produced dramatic cricket. In 2019, India won the ODI series 4–1 — only their second ODI series win in New Zealand since 2009 — but lost the T20Is 1–2. The 2020 tour swung wildly: India whitewashed the T20Is 5–0, the first 5–0 bilateral T20I whitewash ever, then New Zealand returned the favour with a 3–0 ODI whitewash and a 2–0 Test series win.

Diaspora angle

New Zealand's Indian community is one of the country's fastest-growing, and India fixtures routinely draw the largest, loudest crowds of any touring side — though NZC's public framing has emphasised Kiwi fans generally rather than diaspora demand. Either way, an India tour in New Zealand is the closest thing world cricket has to a travelling carnival, and this summer's box office already shows it.

What's next

With 50,000 tickets gone and the first ball still weeks away, NZC is planning "a number of events surrounding the tour" with fan activations at venues, according to Ellis. Tickets remain on general sale, and given the current trajectory, the board may open further capacity at other venues if the Hagley Oval pattern repeats. Expect sell-out signs at several fixtures well before October 22.
nri_angle: India fixtures draw the largest and loudest diaspora crowds of any touring side in New Zealand, home to one of the world's fastest-growing Indian communities.
